How this connects to you

Every game you have ever played runs one loop: something reads your thumbs, code decides what that press means, the screen answers. Press, decide, respond, millions of times a minute. Pro players train that loop on aim trainers, drills that time the gap between seeing and reacting. This program teaches you to build that exact loop with your own hands: something senses, code you wrote decides, something responds. Once you can build the loop, you understand every controller you will ever hold.

Inside a controller: a circuit that reads your thumbs.
What we could build · Reaction Duel
A two player quick-draw rig

The lights run a fake-out countdown. First clean press wins the round, the lights flood the winner's color, the screen keeps score. Press early and the rig catches you and docks a point. You write the countdown, the cheat detection, the scoring. All of it. Stretch: a motion controller you build yourself for a screen game.

You run the game. Your friends lose at it. That is the whole pitch.

The wiring and the how stay for the build sessions, if this is your call.

Watch
Behind the scenes
  • Jerry Lawson, a Black engineer, used circuit design to invent the swappable game cartridge. One engineering decision created the way games are sold to this day.
  • Gunpei Yokoi went from maintaining Nintendo's factory machines to inventing the D-pad. Every controller since has been built on that one input.
  • Professional game testers are paid to break games and write up exactly what failed. That is engineering work, and it is roughly the role on offer here.

How this connects to you

Watch any producer work and you are watching one loop: a pad gets tapped, code decides the sound, the room answers with sound and light. Steve Lacy proved the gear is not the magic. He cut records on a phone. The magic is knowing the chain. This program teaches you to build that chain yourself: your hand or your track as the input, your code deciding, lights and sound answering.

The console is the instrument.
What we could build · Air instrument + reactive rig
A theremin and a sound-reactive light ring

Two machines. The first is an instrument you play by moving your hand in the air: height sets the pitch, tilt bends the note. The second listens to the room and pulses the lights to whatever is playing. Your track, your thresholds, your color map.

Room lights that hit on the drop of your own playlist. Visible on every video call you take.

The wiring and the how stay for the build sessions, if this is your call.

Watch
Behind the scenes
  • Steve Lacy used the phone in his pocket as a studio and produced a track on Kendrick Lamar's DAMN. with it. Knowing the chain beat owning the gear.
  • Young Guru used the mixing console to shape the sound of Jay-Z's records for over twenty years. The artist gets the fame. The engineer builds the sound.
  • J Dilla used a beat machine so precisely that he changed how rhythm gets programmed. That machine now sits in the Smithsonian.

How this connects to you

Elite sport turned into a numbers game. A keeper has under half a second on a penalty, so pros train reactions against flashing light pods that time them to the millisecond, and wear trackers that turn every sprint into data a coach can read. Underneath, it is all one idea: a sensor watches the body, code turns it into a number, the number changes the training. This program teaches you to build your own versions: machines that watch, time, and score you and your friends.

The vest is a tracker. Every sprint becomes data.
What we could build · Pro training rig
A reaction pod that keeps receipts

The lights flash a random color. You kill it with a strike or a hand wave. The screen posts your time in milliseconds and holds the session best. Keepers, fighters, and sprinters train on exactly this category of device. Second build: a jump meter that reads your hang time.

Bring it to practice. Everyone gets a number next to their name. Numbers end arguments.

The wiring and the how stay for the build sessions, if this is your call.

Watch
Behind the scenes
  • Clubs use the vest trackers to decide who trains harder, who rests, who starts on the weekend. The data, not the eye, makes the call.
  • Tennis and football use Hawk-Eye's cameras and code to make calls no referee could make. The technology is trusted over the human eye.
  • Streaming a live match to your phone with almost no delay takes a room full of engineers solving problems in real time.

How this connects to you

What makes Lewis Hamilton's car fast is not one thing you can point at. It is hundreds of sensors feeding a wall of engineers, a steering wheel that is really a computer with more than twenty controls under his thumbs, and launch practice against the same five lights you just faced at the top of this page. Speed is engineered. Strip away the money and it is the same loop this program teaches: something senses, code decides, the machine responds.

Hamilton in the pit lane. The speed is engineered long before the lights go out.
What we could build · Race engineering
Start lights, a steering wheel, and a black box

Three machines. The five-light start rig from the top of this page, in real hardware, with jump-start detection. A steering wheel you build and hold, steering a racing game on screen. And a telemetry black box: strap it to anything that moves, log the forces, then read the graphs like a race engineer. Which pieces of Hamilton's world we recreate, and how, is worked out in the build sessions.

Whoever launches on your lights gets timed. Whoever rides with your black box gets graphed.

The wiring and the how stay for the build sessions, if this is your call.

Watch
Behind the scenes
  • Every lap, hundreds of sensors stream the car's data to the pit wall, and engineers reading those graphs decide strategy mid-race. Speed is a data job.
  • Lewis Hamilton, seven world titles and the only Black driver in the sport's history, funds Mission 44, opening doors into engineering and motorsport for kids the industry overlooks.
  • STEM Racing is a real competition endorsed by Formula 1 where student teams design and race miniature cars. It just arrived in Canada.
